learn: Textual evidence is specific information from a text that supports an analysis: quotations, paraphrases and details.
Strong evidence is directly relevant; weak evidence is only loosely connected to your claim.
Cite evidence with signal phrases ("The narrator reveals...") and page or paragraph numbers.
check: Evidence restated in your own words
Citing a page number helps readers...
lessons.try: Choose a claim about a character and find the strongest piece of evidence for it.

learn: Explicit meaning is stated outright; implicit meaning is suggested and must be inferred.
Authors imply ideas through details, dialogue, and what characters notice or ignore.
Support every inference with at least one piece of textual evidence.
lessons.try: Write an inference about a story's setting with two supporting details.

learn: RACE is a structure for written responses: Restate the question, Answer it, Cite evidence, Explain the evidence.
Explanation is the most important part: show how the evidence proves your answer.
RACE works for both fiction and nonfiction.
check: The C in RACE stands for...
The most important part of RACE is often...
lessons.try: Answer a question about a short story using RACE.

learn: Annotating means marking a text as you read: underlining key lines, circling unknown words and writing questions in the margin.
A simple code helps: ? for confusion, ! for surprise, * for important, and a box for new words.
Annotations turn reading into a conversation and make finding evidence later much faster.
check: A ? in the margin usually marks...
lessons.try: Annotate the first page of "The Gift of the Magi" by O. Henry using the code.

learn: Good readers ask questions before, during and after reading.
"Why did she do that?" and "What will happen next?" keep you engaged.
Some questions are answered in the text; others need inference or research.
check: "What will happen next?" is a ___ question.
lessons.try: Write five questions while reading a chapter of "Black Beauty" and answer three.

learn: What characters say, and how they say it, reveals feelings and motives.
Notice word choice, interruptions, silence and tone tags such as "snapped" or "whispered".
Combine dialogue clues with what you know about people.
check: Silence in a conversation can show...
lessons.try: Infer two characters' feelings from a dialogue passage in "Little Women".

learn: Quotations must be copied exactly, word for word, inside quotation marks.
Use an ellipsis (...) to show you left words out, and brackets [ ] to add a word for clarity.
Never change a quotation's meaning.
lessons.try: Correctly quote three sentences, one using an ellipsis.

learn: Blend quotations into your own sentences instead of dropping them alone.
Example: Jo declares that she will "make a mark" in the world.
Embedded quotes read smoothly and show control.
lessons.try: Rewrite three "dropped" quotations as embedded quotations.

learn: Paraphrasing restates a short passage in your own words, keeping all ideas.
Summarising shortens a long passage to its main points.
Both still need citations.
check: A paraphrase is about ___ the original length.
lessons.try: Paraphrase one paragraph and summarise one chapter.

learn: Not all evidence is equally strong.
The best evidence is specific, relevant and directly proves the point.
Compare two pieces and explain which is stronger.
lessons.try: Rank four quotations by strength for one claim.

learn: After evidence, explain how it supports your claim.
Use phrases: "This shows...", "This suggests...", "Because of this..."
Explanation is where your thinking shows.
lessons.try: Add two sentences of explanation to each of three quotes.

learn: Text-dependent questions can only be answered from the text.
Reread, locate, and cite.
Avoid answers from outside knowledge alone.
check: Text-dependent questions are answered from the...
lessons.try: Answer five text-dependent questions on a story by Washington Irving.

learn: Close reading means slow, repeated reading of a short passage.
First read for gist; second for craft; third for meaning.
Notice word choice, sentence length and structure.
lessons.try: Close read the opening paragraph of "Rip Van Winkle".

learn: In discussions, point to the page: "On page 12, it says..."
Build on others: "Adding to what Sam said..."
Disagree politely with evidence.
lessons.try: Hold a Socratic circle on a short story.

learn: Annotate, question and infer.
Quote accurately and embed smoothly.
Choose and explain the strongest evidence.
check: A summary is ___ than the original.
lessons.try: Write a RACE paragraph on a new passage.

learn: A theme is a message about life or human nature that the text conveys.
Look for how the conflict is resolved, what characters learn and repeated symbols or ideas.
Express themes as complete statements, not single words.
check: A theme is a message about...
lessons.try: Write a theme statement for a novel and identify two details that develop it.

learn: Themes develop over the course of a text through particular details.
Track how a character's choices and their consequences build the theme.
In "The Gift of the Magi" by O. Henry (1905), a couple's sacrifices develop the theme that love means giving.
check: Over the course of a text
Who wrote "The Gift of the Magi"?
That story's theme is that love means...
lessons.try: Read "The Gift of the Magi" and trace how the theme develops.

learn: An objective summary distinguishes the text's ideas from your own opinions.
Include the central idea and the most important supporting points.
Keep it concise, in present tense and in your own words.
check: An objective summary distinguishes the text from...
lessons.try: Summarise an article in under 100 words without opinions.

learn: A topic is a word or phrase: friendship, courage, greed.
A theme is a full statement about that topic: "True friendship requires sacrifice."
Many texts share topics but differ in theme.
check: "Courage means acting despite fear" is a...
lessons.try: Turn five topics into theme statements.

learn: How a conflict is resolved often reveals the theme.
Ask: what did the character learn, and at what cost?
The ending usually carries the message.
check: Theme is often revealed by how the ___ is resolved.
The message is often in the...
lessons.try: Find the theme of "The Gift of the Magi" from its ending.

learn: Symbols are objects that stand for bigger ideas.
A broken watch may symbolise lost time; a light may stand for hope.
Repeated symbols point to themes.
check: A symbol stands for a bigger...
lessons.try: Track one symbol through "The Happy Prince" by Oscar Wilde.

learn: How a character changes signals what the author values.
Compare the character at the start and end.
Ebenezer Scrooge changes from greedy to generous.
check: Compare the character at the ___ and end.
lessons.try: Chart Scrooge's change in "A Christmas Carol".

learn: Rich texts carry more than one theme.
"A Christmas Carol" explores generosity, memory and redemption.
Support each with evidence.
check: Being saved or changed for good
lessons.try: Find two themes in one text and support each.

learn: Universal themes appear across cultures and centuries.
Good versus evil, coming of age, the power of love.
Myths, fables and novels share them.
lessons.try: Find one universal theme in a fable and a novel.

learn: A poem and a story can share a theme.
Compare how each develops it.
Use a Venn diagram.
lessons.try: Compare a theme in a poem and a short story.

learn: Objective summaries leave out opinions and judgements.
Avoid words like "amazing" or "boring".
Report what happens, not how you feel.
lessons.try: Remove opinions from a sample summary.

learn: Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then.
Example: Dorothy wanted to go home, but she was in Oz, so she followed the road, then met the Wizard.
A fast way to capture plot.
lessons.try: Write SWBST summaries for three stories.

learn: Identify the central idea and key supporting points.
Keep the author's order.
Use your own words.
lessons.try: Summarise an article about the Wright brothers.

learn: Topic sentence states the theme.
Two pieces of evidence with explanation.
A concluding sentence ties back.
lessons.try: Write a theme paragraph on a fable.

learn: Topics become themes as statements.
Themes come from conflict, symbols and change.
Summaries are short and objective.
lessons.try: Theme and summary stations.

units.t: Characters, Plot and Point of View

learn: Plot unfolds in episodes as characters respond to conflict.
Internal conflict happens within a character; external conflict is with another character, nature or society.
Characters change in response to events; this change often reveals the theme.
check: A struggle within a character is...
A character versus a storm is...
lessons.try: Identify the internal and external conflicts in a story.

learn: The narrator's point of view determines what readers know.
Dramatic irony occurs when readers know something characters don't.
Authors develop the narrator's perspective through word choice and what is noticed.
check: Dramatic irony is when readers know...
A narrator's perspective is developed through...
lessons.try: Find an example of dramatic irony in a story or film.

learn: Compare texts in different genres on similar themes: a poem and a story about courage.
Note how each form's features shape the message.
Comparing reveals different approaches to the same idea.
check: A poem and a story can share a...
lessons.try: Compare a poem and a short story that share a theme.

learn: Direct: the author tells us ("She was kind").
Indirect: we infer from speech, thoughts, effect on others, actions, looks (STEAL).
Indirect is often richer.
check: STEAL stands for speech, thoughts, effect, actions and...
lessons.try: Find STEAL clues for one character.

learn: Motivation is why a character acts.
Internal (fear, love) or external (a threat, a reward).
Motivation drives plot.
lessons.try: Chart motivations of three characters in "Treasure Island".

learn: The protagonist is the main character.
The antagonist opposes the protagonist.
An antagonist can be a person, nature or society.
lessons.try: Name protagonists and antagonists in five stories.

learn: Character vs character, self, nature, society.
External conflicts are outside; internal are inside the mind.
Many stories mix types.
check: A storm threatening a ship is vs...
lessons.try: Classify conflicts in five scenes.

learn: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
The climax is the turning point of highest tension.
Draw a plot mountain.
check: Events after the climax are the...
lessons.try: Plot "The Monkey's Paw" by W. W. Jacobs on a mountain.

learn: Foreshadowing hints at what's to come.
Flashback shows earlier events.
Both shape suspense and understanding.
check: A hint about the future is...
A scene from the past is a...
lessons.try: Find foreshadowing in "The Monkey's Paw".

learn: Short sentences and cliff-hangers speed pace.
Long descriptions slow it.
Authors control tension.
lessons.try: Rewrite a calm scene to build suspense.

learn: The narrator is a character using "I".
We see only what they know and feel.
They may be unreliable.
lessons.try: Find signs of first person in "Treasure Island" (Jim Hawkins).

learn: Third-person limited follows one character's thoughts.
Third-person omniscient knows everyone's thoughts.
Objective shows only actions and speech.
lessons.try: Identify the point of view in four excerpts.

learn: An unreliable narrator can't be fully trusted.
They may lie, misunderstand or be biased.
Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" narrator insists he is sane.
check: An unreliable narrator can't be fully...
lessons.try: Find evidence the narrator is unreliable.

learn: The same event can look different from two characters.
Retelling changes meaning.
Compare tone and details.
check: Changing point of view can change...
Retelling from the villain's view is a new...
lessons.try: Retell a fairy tale from the villain's view.

learn: Characterisation, motivation and conflict drive plot.
Plot structure, foreshadowing and suspense.
Point of view shapes what we know.
lessons.try: Story elements escape room.

learn: Similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole and idioms create meaning beyond the literal.
An extended metaphor carries a comparison through many lines.
Emily Dickinson's "'Hope' is the thing with feathers" compares hope to a bird throughout.
lessons.try: Read Dickinson's poem and list every detail of the extended metaphor.

learn: Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling or association a word carries.
"Thrifty" and "stingy" have similar denotations but different connotations: positive and negative.
Writers choose words carefully for connotation.
check: A word's dictionary meaning is its...
lessons.try: List three pairs of words with similar denotations but different connotations.

learn: Tone is the author's attitude toward the subject: humorous, serious, sarcastic, nostalgic.
Mood is the feeling the reader experiences: tense, peaceful, gloomy.
Word choice and imagery create both tone and mood.
lessons.try: Rewrite a calm paragraph to create a tense mood.

learn: Similes compare with like or as; metaphors say one thing is another.
Authors use them to make images vivid.
Ask what qualities are being compared.
check: "The classroom was a zoo" is a...
lessons.try: Find five comparisons in "The Call of the Wild" and explain them.

learn: Personification gives human traits to things: "The wind howled."
Hyperbole exaggerates for effect: "I've told you a million times."
Both add emotion.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph using both.

learn: Idioms are expressions not meant literally: "break the ice".
Allusions refer to famous stories: "a Herculean task".
Both need background knowledge.
lessons.try: Explain ten idioms and three allusions.

learn: Imagery appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
Strong images help readers feel present.
Look for sensory words.
check: "The bread smelled warm and sweet" appeals to...
lessons.try: Highlight imagery by sense in a passage.

learn: Denotation is the dictionary meaning.
Connotation is the feeling a word carries.
"Thrifty" (positive) vs "cheap" (negative).
lessons.try: Sort word pairs by connotation.

learn: Tone is the author's attitude: playful, serious, bitter.
Word choice creates tone.
Change words, change tone.
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph in two tones.

learn: Mood is how the reader feels.
Setting details create mood.
Poe's dark, dreary settings create dread.
lessons.try: Find mood words in "The Fall of the House of Usher" opening.

learn: Definition, synonym, antonym, example clues.
"Unlike his gregarious sister, Tom was shy."
Antonym clue: gregarious means sociable.
check: "Unlike his gregarious sister, Tom was shy." Gregarious means...
lessons.try: Solve ten tricky words from context.

learn: bio (life), graph (write), tele (far), port (carry), dict (say).
Roots unlock thousands of words.
Biography = life writing.
lessons.try: Build twenty words from five roots.

learn: Word analogies show relationships: hot : cold :: up : down.
Types: antonym, synonym, part-whole, tool-use.
Find the relationship first.
lessons.try: Solve ten analogies.

learn: Name the device, quote it, explain its effect.
"Poe's repetition of 'dreary' creates a mood of gloom."
Effect is the key part.
check: Name the device, quote it, explain its...
lessons.try: Write an author's craft paragraph.

learn: Figurative language, imagery, tone and mood.
Connotation and roots.
Explain effects.
lessons.try: Figurative language scavenger hunt.

units.t: Reading Nonfiction: Main Idea and Structure

learn: The central idea is the main point of a nonfiction text.
Authors develop it through examples, facts, anecdotes and explanations.
Trace how each section contributes to the central idea.
check: Each section should contribute to the...
lessons.try: Outline how an article develops its central idea section by section.

learn: Authors use structure to support purpose: chronological for history, problem-solution for proposals.
A section, chapter or paragraph fits into the overall structure.
Analyse why the author placed information where they did.
lessons.try: Explain why an author began an article with a surprising anecdote.

lessons.t: Author's Point of View and Purpose
learn: An author's purpose may be to inform, persuade, entertain or explain.
Point of view is the author's position on the topic.
Identify how the author distinguishes their position from others.
check: Point of view in nonfiction is the author's...
lessons.try: Find an editorial and identify the author's purpose and point of view.

learn: Each paragraph usually has one central idea.
Often in the first sentence, sometimes the last.
Details support it.
check: A paragraph usually has ___ central idea.
The central idea is often in the ___ sentence.
lessons.try: Underline central ideas in five paragraphs.

lessons.t: Central Idea of a Whole Text
learn: Combine paragraph ideas into one big idea.
Check the title, introduction and conclusion.
State it in one sentence.
check: State the central idea in ___ sentence.
lessons.try: Find the central idea of a biography of Marie Curie.

learn: Headings, captions, bold words, diagrams and sidebars.
They help readers navigate and understand.
Read them before the text.
lessons.try: Do a text feature walk through a science article.

learn: Events in time order.
Signal words: first, then, in 1903, finally.
Common in history and biographies.
lessons.try: Make a timeline from an article about the Wright brothers.

learn: Explains why things happen.
Signal words: because, so, as a result, therefore.
One cause can have many effects.
lessons.try: Make a cause-effect chain from an article on the Dust Bowl.

learn: Shows similarities and differences.
Signal words: similarly, however, both, unlike.
Block or point-by-point organisation.
lessons.try: Compare frogs and toads from an article.

learn: Describes a problem and one or more solutions.
Signal words: the problem is, one solution, to fix this.
Evaluate whether solutions work.
lessons.try: Evaluate solutions in an article about clean water.

learn: Persuade, Inform, Entertain.
Many texts mix purposes.
Look at word choice and structure.
check: PIE stands for persuade, inform and...
lessons.try: Sort ten texts by main purpose.

lessons.t: Author's Point of View in Nonfiction
learn: Authors reveal views through word choice and evidence chosen.
Compare two articles on the same topic.
Notice what is left out.
lessons.try: Compare two articles about zoos.

learn: Primary: created at the time (letters, photos, diaries).
Secondary: written later about events (textbooks).
Both are useful.
check: A diary from 1863 is a ___ source.
Photos taken at an event are...
lessons.try: Sort ten sources.

lessons.t: Reading Graphs and Charts in Articles
learn: Graphs support claims with data.
Read titles, labels and keys.
Connect the graph to the text.
lessons.try: Explain how a graph supports an article.

learn: Central idea and supporting details.
Five text structures.
Purpose, point of view and sources.
lessons.try: Nonfiction structure sort.

learn: An argument states a clear claim and supports it with reasons and evidence.
A claim is debatable: reasonable people could disagree.
Each reason should be supported with relevant evidence.
lessons.try: Write a claim about whether students should have phones in school, with three reasons.

learn: Credible sources are accurate, current and written by knowledgeable authors.
Types of evidence: statistics, expert testimony, examples and anecdotes.
Cite sources so readers can check them.
check: Which is a type of evidence?
lessons.try: Find two credible sources that support your claim.

learn: Organise an argument: introduction with claim, body paragraphs with reasons, conclusion.
Use transitions like "furthermore", "in addition" and "as a result".
The conclusion restates the claim and leaves the reader with something to think about.
lessons.try: Draft a five-paragraph argument essay.

learn: A fact can be proven; an opinion is a belief.
A claim is an arguable position that can be supported with reasons and evidence.
"School should start at 9 a.m." is a claim.
check: "Water boils at 100 °C at sea level" is a...
lessons.try: Sort twelve statements into fact, opinion and claim.

learn: A strong claim is specific, arguable and focused.
Weak: "Homework is bad." Strong: "Schools should limit homework to 30 minutes a night."
It guides the whole essay.
lessons.try: Revise five weak claims.

learn: Reasons answer "Why?"
Each reason gets its own paragraph.
Three strong reasons beat six weak ones.
lessons.try: Brainstorm reasons for a claim and choose the best three.

learn: Facts, statistics, expert quotes, examples and anecdotes.
Statistics and experts are often strongest.
Mix types for variety.
check: "Doctors recommend 9 hours of sleep" is an ___ quote.
A short personal story is an...
lessons.try: Find one of each type for a claim.

learn: Check author, date, purpose and evidence.
.gov, .edu and established publishers are often reliable.
Be wary of anonymous or very old sources for current topics.
check: An anonymous blog is often ___ credible.
lessons.try: Rate five sources for credibility.

learn: A counterclaim is the opposing view.
Acknowledge it fairly: "Some argue that..."
Then respond with a rebuttal.
lessons.try: Write a counterclaim paragraph.

learn: Show why the counterclaim is weaker.
Use evidence, not insults.
"However, research shows..."
check: A rebuttal shows why the counterclaim is...
lessons.try: Write rebuttals for three counterclaims.

learn: Hooks: a question, startling fact, short anecdote or quote.
Give background, then state the claim.
Claim usually ends the introduction.
check: A startling fact can be a...
lessons.try: Write three different hooks for one essay.

learn: Furthermore, in addition, on the other hand, consequently.
Transitions connect ideas.
Vary them.
lessons.try: Add transitions to a choppy essay.

learn: Avoid slang, contractions and "you".
Use precise, academic words.
Keep a respectful tone.
lessons.try: Formalise a casual paragraph.

learn: Restate the claim in new words.
Summarise reasons.
End with a call to action or big idea.
check: A call to action asks readers to...
Avoid adding ___ evidence in a conclusion.
lessons.try: Write a persuasive conclusion.

learn: Claim, reasons, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal.
Credible sources and formal style.
Persuasive conclusions.
check: A credible source has a known...
lessons.try: Write and peer-review a full argument essay.

learn: Informative writing explains a topic clearly with facts and examples.
A strong introduction hooks the reader and previews the main points.
A thesis statement states the main idea of the essay.
check: The main idea of the essay
lessons.try: Write an introduction with a hook and thesis for an essay on volcanoes.

learn: Group related information into paragraphs with topic sentences.
Use structures like definition, classification, compare-contrast and cause-effect.
Headings, graphics and multimedia can aid understanding.
lessons.try: Organise notes on a topic into three categories with headings.

learn: Use precise vocabulary and domain-specific terms.
Maintain a formal style: avoid slang and "I think".
Vary sentence structure for interest and clarity.
lessons.try: Revise a paragraph to make it more formal and precise.

learn: Start broad, then narrow: Animals → Desert animals → How camels survive heat.
A narrow topic is easier to cover well.
Ask: can I explain this in five paragraphs?
check: Narrow topics are easier to cover...
lessons.try: Narrow three broad topics.

learn: Good research questions are open and focused.
"How did the Hohokam move water?" beats "Did the Hohokam have water?"
Questions guide note-taking.
check: "Did they have water?" is a ___ question.
lessons.try: Write five research questions.

learn: Use bullet points and key words, not full sentences.
Record the source for each note.
Put quotation marks around exact words.
lessons.try: Take notes from two sources.

learn: Plagiarism is using someone's words or ideas without credit.
Paraphrase and cite.
It is dishonest and can fail you.
lessons.try: Fix three plagiarised sentences.

learn: The thesis states the topic and main points.
"Camels survive heat by storing fat, conserving water and resisting sun."
It maps the essay.
check: A thesis states the topic and...
lessons.try: Write a thesis for your topic.

learn: Headings divide sections.
Each section covers one main point.
Readers can skim.
lessons.try: Add headings to a draft.

learn: Define technical terms clearly.
Give examples to show meaning.
"Photosynthesis, the process plants use to make food, ..."
lessons.try: Define and give examples for five terms.

learn: Diagrams, charts and tables support explanations.
Label clearly and refer to them in the text.
Choose the right graphic.
check: A process is best shown with a...
lessons.try: Add a diagram and caption to your essay.

learn: Use exact words: "sprinted" not "went fast".
Use subject vocabulary: "habitat", "adaptation".
Avoid vague words like "stuff" and "things".
lessons.try: Replace ten vague words.

lessons.t: Citing Sources in a Works Cited List
learn: List each source: author, title, publisher, date.
Alphabetise by author's last name.
Match in-text citations.
check: Works cited lists are alphabetised by...
lessons.try: Create a works cited list for three sources.

learn: Read aloud to find confusing parts.
Cut repeated words.
Check each paragraph supports the thesis.
lessons.try: Revise a peer's draft for clarity.

learn: Narrow topic, research, notes, thesis.
Organise, define, illustrate and cite.
Revise for clarity.
lessons.try: Publish an informative article.

learn: Start a narrative by establishing context and a narrator or point of view.
Openings can begin with action, dialogue or a vivid description.
Introduce the main character and hint at the conflict.
lessons.try: Write three different opening lines for the same story.

learn: Dialogue, pacing and description develop experiences and characters.
Pacing controls speed: slow down for important moments, speed up for transitions.
Flashback shows past events; foreshadowing hints at future events.
lessons.try: Add a flashback to a story you've written.

learn: Use precise words and sensory details to convey experiences.
Transition words signal shifts in time and setting.
The conclusion should follow from the events and reflect on them.
lessons.try: Revise a scene to add five sensory details.

learn: Start with a "what if?" question.
Use memories, objects or photos as sparks.
Keep an idea notebook.
check: A good spark is a "what ___?" question.
lessons.try: Write ten "what if?" questions.

learn: Give characters a want, a fear and a flaw.
Show traits through action.
A character sketch helps.
check: Characters need a want, a fear and a...
lessons.try: Write a character sketch.

learn: Setting is time and place.
Use sensory detail.
Setting can create conflict (a storm, a desert).
lessons.try: Describe a setting with all five senses.

learn: Use a story mountain to plan.
One main conflict.
Know your ending before you start.
check: A short story has ___ main conflict.
lessons.try: Plan a story on a mountain chart.

learn: Tell: "She was scared." Show: "Her hands shook as she reached for the door."
Showing lets readers infer.
Use action and detail.
lessons.try: Rewrite five "tell" sentences.

learn: New speaker, new paragraph.
Punctuation goes inside quotation marks.
Dialogue reveals character.
lessons.try: Write a dialogue scene of ten lines.

learn: Slow down important moments with detail.
Speed through less important parts.
Use scene breaks to jump time.
lessons.try: Expand one key moment and summarise one dull one.

learn: "The dog went" → "The terrier bolted."
Precise nouns create pictures.
Strong verbs create movement.
lessons.try: Revise a paragraph with strong verbs.

lessons.t: Writing in Different Points of View
learn: Try first person for closeness.
Try third person for a wider view.
Stay consistent.
lessons.try: Rewrite a scene in a new point of view.

learn: Resolve the main conflict.
Show how the character changed.
Avoid "it was all a dream".
check: An ending should resolve the main...
lessons.try: Write two possible endings and choose the stronger.

learn: Give praise, a question and a suggestion.
Be specific and kind.
Revise using feedback.
check: Feedback includes praise, a question and a...
lessons.try: Workshop a classmate's story.

learn: Characters, setting, plot.
Show don't tell, dialogue, pacing.
Strong endings.
lessons.try: Publish a short story.

learn: Subjective pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) are subjects. Objective pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) are objects.
"Maya and I went" is correct; "Me and Maya went" is not.
Avoid vague pronouns: "When Tom met Sam, he smiled" is unclear about who smiled.
check: Makes it unclear who is meant
lessons.try: Fix five sentences with pronoun errors.

learn: Commas, parentheses and dashes set off nonrestrictive elements: "My brother, who lives in Ohio, called."
Dashes add emphasis; parentheses de-emphasise.
Semicolons join closely related independent clauses.
lessons.try: Write sentences using a dash, parentheses and a semicolon.

learn: Simple sentences have one independent clause. Compound sentences join two with a conjunction.
Complex sentences have an independent and a dependent clause.
Mixing sentence types improves flow and interest.
check: An independent and a dependent clause
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph using all three sentence types.

learn: Subject: I, he, she, we, they. Object: me, him, her, us, them.
"She and I went." "Mom gave it to her and me."
Remove the other person to test.
check: ___ and I went to the park.
lessons.try: Choose pronouns in fifteen sentences.

learn: Mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs.
No apostrophes: "its" not "it's" for possession.
"It's" means "it is".
lessons.try: Fix its/it's errors in a paragraph.

learn: Reflexive: "She hurt herself." (needed)
Intensive: "I myself saw it." (for emphasis; can be removed)
Don't use them as subjects: "Myself went" is wrong.
lessons.try: Label reflexive and intensive pronouns.

learn: Pronouns match their antecedent in number.
"Each student brought his or her book" or rephrase with plural.
